Ray's update, with the numbers behind it

What I've been working on, and what I learned

I want Kong Royale to run smoothly for everyone, on any laptop and in any browser, Safari too, without crashing mid-match. So every change has to be proven on real machines before it ships, and every number on this page says where it came from.

  • measured measured on a real machine
  • model from a network model, not a real network yet
  • estimate an estimate, not measured yet

Now

  • Ship the Safari descent fixes (#317, #318, #320) to stable as kong-v1.3.1 once the Safari memory check (RAY-278) clears.
  • Frame rate: build the static draw-list replay (about 2–2.6 ms of the ~21 ms main thread on RTX), one location at a time behind ?drawlist=1, with identical pixels.
  • Fix what live play showed: Safari spikes in the plane and tuk-tuk, and Firefox at 16 fps on Apple Silicon (RAY-280).
  • Turn on automatic performance summaries for every player after RAY-278, so real-player data drives the next fixes.
  • Upstream: batch 16 sends ~60 fork PRs to Max, and the fork stays synced.

Biggest wins

Safari finishes a whole match on a 16 GB Mac

measured
8.5→7.3GB peak

from reaching the limit to finishing the match

Before
Reached Safari's limit 82 s after landing, at 8.5 GB
Now
Reaches the results screen, peaking at 6.9 to 7.3 GB

Safari gives one tab about 8.5 GB on a 16 GB Mac, and I set out to fit inside that. The game now keeps at most 4 far-away locations loaded instead of 10, and a full match ends on the results screen.

How I know

measured on a real machine, 2026-11-05

Mac mini M4 16 GB, Safari, main 3248912 (2 runs) against main 1ee1f52 (1 run); tools/dashboard/story.json, project drive handoffs/safari-growth/pr160/README.md

Changes: #140, #149, #157, #160

Tuk-tuks draw in fewer pieces

measured
113→47draws per tuk-tuk

2.4× fewer

Before
113 meshes, 82 of them casting shadows
Now
47 meshes, 32 casting shadows, same triangles

Tuk-tuks were the biggest source of draw calls on my test route. Each part was split into pieces for no visual reason, so I merged each part into one mesh per material.

How I know

measured on a real machine, 2026-11-06

Mesh count in client/src/actors/tuktuk.ts, with same-camera stills (2 of 3 views identical, 1 pixel differs in the third); Captain drive reports/KONG-68.md

Changes: #220

The Murk's tree crowns draw in one go

measured
~170→~10draws, seen from Mango Market

about 17× fewer

Before
About 170 draws a frame for the crowns
Now
About 10: one multi-draw per pass

Each 36 m cell of crowns was three meshes. I batched the cells, so the whole canopy is one draw per pass.

How I know

measured on a real machine, 2026-11-06

Draw counts from Mango Market; on an RTX laptop walk-town draws went 655 to 513 (p50) with frame times inside the run-to-run spread; Captain drive handoffs/upstream/batch14/murk/bodies/murk-crown-batch.md

Changes: #234

Safari at High is smoother

measured
36.3→46.6fps

+28.4%

Before
36.3 fps, 157 frames over 33 ms
Now
46.6 fps (43.3 to 47.9), 22 frames over 33 ms

At High on a Retina screen, Safari's frame lands just past 16.7 ms and snaps to 30 fps. The fix lowers only the 3D resolution while the game misses the refresh, then raises it again.

How I know

measured on a real machine, 2026-11-06

Safari 27.0.1 on a Mac, High, DPR 2, main 9cc83fa (n=4) against the PR (n=5); Captain drive reports/KONG-82.md

Changes: #265

Inputs keep flowing on a lossy connection

measured (emulated network path)
214→48.2ms of input delay beyond ping, slowest 1%

4.4× fewer

Before
214 ms on WebSockets at 250 ms ping and 1% loss (108 ms at 150 ms ping)
Now
48.2 ms on WebTransport (48.8 ms at 150 ms ping)

On WebSockets one lost packet holds up every input behind it. The new optional WebTransport path sends every unacknowledged input in each packet, so the next packet repairs a lost one. These runs used real network stacks over an emulated path; next is the real-player A/B.

How I know

measured on a real machine, 2026-11-06

Netpath matrix: real kernel TCP and QUIC over an emulated path, n=10 per arm (9 or 10 completed), main d83729f, ack minus RTT p99; project drive handoffs/KONG-wt/netpath/2026-11-06-d83729f/netpath-matrix.md

Changes: #227, #228, #231, #254

Low-memory mode uses 40% less graphics memory

measured
3,141→1,894MB of graphics memory at the title

−39.7%

Before
3,141 MB by default (4,206 MB in the plane)
Now
1,894 MB in low-memory mode (2,226 MB in the plane)

Low-memory mode at first only waited to load far-away areas. It now frees them and draws a cheap stand-in, so Safari keeps at most 4 far-away locations loaded instead of 10.

How I know

measured on a real machine, 2026-11-06

Mac mini M4, Metal, WebGL MB, farimp re-gate 2 (KONG-54), main fbe5559; project drive handoffs/farimp-regate2-metal/

Changes: #107, #149, #160

Less memory held twice

measured
219→138MB of shape copies in a match

−37%

Before
219 MB kept in main memory after upload
Now
138 MB with ?geofree=1

Meshes kept a copy of their shape in main memory after the graphics card had it. They now drop it and rebuild it only if the browser resets the graphics. It has been on by default since #268, and ?geofree=0 turns it off. The 138 MB figure was measured before that, on a cloud machine with no graphics card; a real-GPU number with it on is still to come.

How I know

measured on a real machine, 2026-11-06

SwiftShader on a cloud machine, tools/performance/memory.mts; project drive handoffs/geofree-default/README.md (PR #268, merged)

What I learned along the way

One thread isn't really the wall

measured

Every WebGL engine sends its draw calls from one JavaScript thread, three.js included. But the browser already does the heavy driver work in its own GPU process, and the WebGL calls are only about 10% of my main thread. What fills it is my own code around each draw: about 16 µs a draw on my RTX laptop and 12 µs on the Mac mini, against about 1.5 µs for plain three.js in a benchmark. That gap is mine to fix.

My game, Mac mini

Plain three.js

Small wins hide in the noise

measured

A 5-run frame-time test can't see a change smaller than about 5%. So I price each idea with a profile and object counts before I spend GPU time on it, and a PR can say "no clear change" and still be a real saving.

±5% noise
Safari High fps (#265) +28.4%
Freezing static scene nodes +1.2%
-5%0%+5%+10%+20%+30%

The same effect costs different amounts on different machines

estimate

The light rays are nearly free on my RTX laptop but likely cost a few ms on a Mac at Retina resolution. In Safari that can be the difference between 60 and 30 fps, because frames snap to the screen's refresh. These are estimates: there is no per-pass GPU timer yet, and adding one is on my list.

RTX laptop, 1080p
≤0.2
Base M-series Mac, 1080p
0.3–1
Mac at Retina (DPR 2)
1–3

ms per frameone 60 Hz frame (16.7)

Where this comes from

an estimate, not measured yet, 2026-11-06

Fetch counts for the quarter-resolution light-ray pass in client/src/world/atmos/post.ts; Captain drive reports/KONG-89.md

Safari plays by its own rules

measured

Safari caps how much memory one tab can use: around 8.5 GB on a 16 GB Mac, where I saw tabs reach the limit at 8.4 to 8.8 GB. Its frame timing even fooled my refresh-rate detection, so I fixed that too.

  • Before: 8.5 GB
  • Now: 7.3 GB
  • Safari's limit, about 8.5 GB
Where this comes from

measured on a real machine, 2026-11-05

Safari page memory on a Mac mini M4 16 GB; tools/dashboard/story.json; the limit range from Captain drive reports/KONG-62.md

Freeing memory takes ownership

measured

Low-memory mode at first only waited to load far-away areas, so after a few km you were back to full memory. It now frees far areas and draws a cheap stand-in in their place.

Before a release goes stable

  1. A smoke test: the title loads with no errors, a bot match starts, the Firing Range works
  2. A frame-time and load comparison against the last stable release
  3. A full Safari match on a 16 GB Mac for memory
  4. A two-player online match

Why so many PRs

I keep each change small and doing one thing, so it's easy to review, measure and roll back. Every PR runs the full check suite, the CI jobs and an AI review before it can land, and the numbers on this dashboard come from those checks.

Mac with 16 GB

Measured on a Mac mini with an M4 chip and 16 GB, in Safari and in Chrome. Since v0.6 a full match finishes in Safari: the game now keeps at most four streamed locations at a time, and Safari's page peaks about 1.3 GB under Safari's limit.

Peak memory in a match

v0.2.0 is the shared starting point of both projects. The fork set out to fit a full Safari match inside the limit Safari sets on a 16 GB Mac, and from v0.6 the match fits: across the checks the page peaked between 6.8 and 7.7 GB against a limit of about 8.4 GB (one v0.6.1 run on a longer route reached 8.3 GB and still finished). Main at 0c1713f was measured in both browsers, two runs each way. In Chrome the low-memory setup cuts the peak from 10.9 to 8.0 GB at 60 fps. In Safari the flags change nothing measurable, because Safari already runs the low-memory path. Chrome doesn't close tabs this way, so its line shows how much it asks of the Mac. The main points use a pixel ratio of 1, the v1.0 Safari point forced 2, so the two aren't a like-for-like change.

How it was measured
  • first Safari baseline. Mac mini, Apple M4, 16 GB, macOS 27, Safari 27. Cold Safari start, prod build, seed 42, 3 runs per build. Memory as Activity Monitor counts it (footprint). Every run reached Safari's limit on this 16 GB Mac, so the value is the size at the title.

    Captain drive: reports/KONG-49 and renders/KONG-49

  • Safari acceptance. Mac mini, Apple M4, 16 GB, macOS 27, Safari 27. Safari acceptance: cold start, prod build, seed 42, low-memory mode on (Safari's default), the kong left standing, a full match. Value is the highest page-process (WebContent) footprint; the whisker spans the 3 runs.

    KONG-54's acceptance report to the Captain, 2026-11-05

  • Safari growth trace. Mac mini, Apple M4, 16 GB, macOS 27, Safari 27. Safari growth trace: prod build, seed 42, low-memory mode on (Safari's default), an autopilot that drops and runs between locations, footprint sampled every 5 s until the results screen or until Safari closes the tab. WebGL and copy counters come from the memory probe injected before the game's scripts.

    project drive: handoffs/safari-growth (KONG-54)

  • Safari release check. Mac mini, Apple M4, 16 GB, macOS 27, Safari 27.0.1. Release check on the Mac: prod build of the tag, seed 42, Auto quality (it picked Low), the moving autopilot through a full match to the results screen, peak footprint per phase. v0.6 ran at the display's own pixel ratio of 1; from v1.0 the check forces a Retina pixel ratio of 2, which draws more pixels, so v1.0 is not lower because of that.

    Kong Mini's release checks (renders/v060, v061, v100, v101 in its drive), as reported to the Captain

  • whole-browser flight, Mac mini (RAY-227). Mac mini, Apple M4, 16 GB, macOS 27.0.1, Chrome 154.0.8037.57 on Metal, Safari 27.0.1. Prod build of fork main 0c1713f on a local server, DPR 1 at a 1080p surface, Auto quality, seed 42, the moving autopilot (v7) from the drop to the results screen, a full practice match per run. n=2 per arm, interleaved, each in a fresh browser process. Arm A is the defaults, arm B adds ?lowmem=1&geofree=1&farimp=1; both add &resaudit. Chrome is the sum of footprint over the Chrome process tree from the automation browser's main process; Safari is WebContent (max) and whole Safari (Safari, WebContent and WebKit GPU processes). Sampled every 2.5 s, peak kept. Notes: the first Chrome pass sampled the wrong process and was discarded and rerun; the Metal shader cache was not wiped between runs; the Mac also runs other work, so the operating system share (below) is an upper bound.

    project drive: handoffs/mem-12gb (RAY-227), measured by KONG-54

  • estimate or plan. Worked out from the measurements named in the note. Estimate or plan, not a measurement. The note gives the arithmetic and its sources.

    docs/memory-architecture.md, Captain drive reports/KONG-44, KONG-47 and KONG-62

Graphics memory (WebGL) at the title and in the plane

The low-memory setup holds about 1.2 GB less than the defaults at the title and about 2 GB less in the plane, because it builds each location only as the player gets near it. Mac with 12 GB or 10 GB

Not measured on a 12 GB or 10 GB Mac. The game's footprint is the same whatever the Mac has, so this chart sets the 16 GB Mac mini's measurements against how much a smaller Mac would have left for the browser. That headroom is an estimate: the operating system's share was read from the Mini's own idle state, 6.1 to 8.1 GB, median 6.5 GB. It is an upper bound for the system's share, because the Mini was also running other work and about 2 GB of swap. A clean system was not measured.

Peak memory against estimated headroom for 12 GB and 10 GB

At the measured system share, nothing fits without swapping. Chrome's low-memory setup (8.0 GB) is over by 2.5 GB on 12 GB and 4.5 GB on 10 GB; Safari's whole browser (8.0 to 8.8 GB) is over by 2.0 to 3.3 GB on 12 GB. Fitting 12 GB takes about 2.5 GB less than Chrome's low-memory setup, and 10 GB about 4.5 GB less; with 1 GB to spare, about 3.5 GB and 5.5 GB. Memory pressure reached "warn" in both Chrome defaults runs and all four Safari runs, and stayed normal in both Chrome low-memory runs.

  • Safari, page process (measured on 16 GB)
  • Safari, whole browser (measured on 16 GB)
  • Chrome, whole browser (measured on 16 GB)
  • Chrome, whole browser, low-memory setup (measured on 16 GB)
  • Safari, whole browser, low-memory flags (measured on 16 GB)
  • 12 GB Mac: about 5.5 GB left for the browser (system share 6.5 GB, an upper bound) (estimate)
  • 10 GB Mac: about 3.5 GB left for the browser (same system share) (estimate)

The 16 GB Mac mini's peaks from the chart above (n=2 each, main at 0c1713f). Only the headroom lines are estimated: 12 GB less the 6.5 GB median system share is 5.5 GB, and 10 GB less it is 3.5 GB. If a smaller Mac's system share were about 3.5 GB (a rough figure that was not measured), headroom would be 8.5 GB and 6.5 GB, Chrome's low-memory setup (8.0 GB) and Safari (8.0 to 8.2 GB on defaults; 7.5 to 8.8 GB with the flags, where one run is over) would fit on 12 GB with 0.5 GB or less to spare (Safari's lowest run, 7.5 GB, would leave 1.0 GB), and nothing would fit on 10 GB. On a real small Mac the system would compress and swap and the footprints would shrink somewhat, so this shows how close the game is, not what a player would see.

Chrome is the sum of footprint over the Chrome process tree from the automation browser's main process; Safari is WebContent (max) and whole Safari (Safari, WebContent and WebKit GPU processes). Windows PC (Chrome on Direct3D 11)

Measured on a Windows PC with an NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X and 30 GB, in Chrome. Windows doesn't close the tab at a fixed size, so the line to watch is the plan's target of under 4 GB. The whole browser is about 2 GB below the shared starting point, v0.2.0. It hasn't been measured this way since v0.5; the release checks for v0.6 and v1.0 timed loading and frames instead.

Peak memory in a match, whole browser

On Auto, v0.2.0 (the shared starting point) starts at Ultra quality on this PC and later builds start at High, so about 0.35 GB of the drop to v0.5 is likely the quality change and the rest came from releases (an estimate across two days of runs). The low-memory setup only saves memory early on: until v0.6 added letting go of far locations it kept every one it built, so after about 4 km of walking it held as much as the defaults.

Phones and tablets not supported yet

Not supported yet. Since v0.6.1, phones and tablets get a "desktop only for now" screen with a button to copy the link, shown before the game loads so the tab never runs out of memory (#195). A phone version needs two things: the game under about 1.2 GB at its peak (an estimate from WebKit's limits on iPhone, about a quarter of today's Safari page at the title) and touch controls, which the game doesn't have yet.

How it's built

I wrote this page so anyone can learn the stack from the angle they care about, from the network to how the rules are modelled to what runs in the browser. Each section has a short explanation, a diagram, and the checks that guard it on every PR. The formal-model diagrams and the checks table are generated from the repo's own files every time the dashboard is built, so they can't drift from the code.

Built from: ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/memory-architecture.md, docs/statecharts/, tools/formal/, tools/run-tests.mjs and .github/workflows/ci.yml. Jump to: The stack at a glance · Networking · Determinism · Runtime and memory · Formal models · What guards every PR

The stack at a glance

Kong Royale has three parts: the browser game in client/, a Node server in server/, and shared/, which holds the game rules and the network protocol. The server and the browser both run the same shared/ code, so the browser can predict what the server will decide.

The server is authoritative. It decides hits, damage, loot, the storm and who wins; the client predicts and asks. In practice mode there is no server: the browser runs the same Match and MatchHost classes itself behind the same link interface, so practice exercises exactly the code an online match does.

What checks it

  • wire / matrix / geometry / http / splat parity Five checks, each asserted against its own expected result: network snapshots, the matrix cache, the geometry index, static file serving and splat viewport selection.
  • headless match (seed 42) A headless 50-bot match with no winner, friendly-fire hits, bots not arming up, tick cost over budget, a vehicle seat and its rider disagreeing, an illegal phase change, or a final state hash that differs from the recorded one.
  • no-GPU boot smoke A production build that doesn't boot in software-rendered Chromium (smoke only, not frame rate or looks), or holds more memory at the title than its budget.

Files: client/src/game/client.ts client/src/game/net.ts shared/net/host.ts shared/net/proto.ts shared/sim/match.ts server/index.ts

Source: ARCHITECTURE.md, "The big picture" and "The match loop"

Networking

The fast path (inputs, snapshots, events) is binary and every frame decodes on its own, so a late player can pick up from any frame. Prediction means my kong never waits for the server: the client steps it with the same stepPlayer the server uses, sends the input, and stores the result under its sequence number. Each snapshot carries the server's exact state after the last input it processed. If that matches the prediction nothing happens; if not, the client restores the server's state and replays the inputs the server hasn't seen yet.

Today's default is two WebSockets per player, first copy wins. WebTransport is optional: a server started with KR_WT=1 can put a share of players (KR_WT_SHARE) on it as an A/B test, a tab keeps its arm, and ?wt=1 or ?wt=0 overrides it. If the session can't be had, or closes later, the player falls back to WebSockets. Over datagrams nothing is resent, so each tick the client sends every input the snapshots haven't acknowledged yet, and a lost packet is repaired by the next one.

What checks it

  • network tails (against tools/performance/net-budgets.json) A network tail (slowest 1% of input replies) that gets worse.
  • WebTransport endpoint (loopback, Node client) The WebTransport endpoint: off by default, refused on a wrong token or a second session, inputs and snapshots as datagrams with lost windows repaired, a session that floods the server being closed, and the A/B arm counted in /health.
  • WebTransport in a browser (loopback, headless Chromium; SKIP without one) WebTransport in headless Chromium against a real server: arm selection, ping and pong, the session outliving a quiet period, fallback to WebSockets when the server closes it, and the flag overrides. It passes with SKIP when no browser or QUIC build is present.
  • WebTransport A/B split by arm (playtest bundles, /health) Bundles not split by transport arm with the right medians and per-minute rates, a link counted twice, or a callsign or message reaching the output.
  • wire / matrix / geometry / http / splat parity Five checks, each asserted against its own expected result: network snapshots, the matrix cache, the geometry index, static file serving and splat viewport selection.

Determinism

Everything in shared/ has to give the same answer in Node and in every browser, or the client's prediction drifts from the server's truth. So shared/ uses no DOM or Node APIs, no wall-clock time in game logic, and no Math.random: all randomness comes from the seeded Rng. The math functions that differ in the last bit between CPUs (sin, cos, pow and friends) go through dmath.ts, which is checked bit for bit against recorded vectors.

The proof is a hash. A headless 50-bot match with a fixed seed runs in npm test, and its final state hash must not change unless the rules changed on purpose. Hot paths such as stepPlayer, collision and hit tests also allocate nothing per tick,.

What checks it

  • lint Shared code that isn't deterministic, per-tick allocation in hot files, unowned GPU resources, raw URL flags, type-only imports written as values.
  • deterministic math (shared/sim/dmath.ts) A math function that gives different bits than the recorded vectors, which would split client and server.
  • headless match (seed 42) A headless 50-bot match with no winner, friendly-fire hits, bots not arming up, tick cost over budget, a vehicle seat and its rider disagreeing, an illegal phase change, or a final state hash that differs from the recorded one.
  • wire / matrix / geometry / http / splat parity Five checks, each asserted against its own expected result: network snapshots, the matrix cache, the geometry index, static file serving and splat viewport selection.

Runtime and memory

The browser holds a lot at once, so every GPU texture, render target and worker has an owner: a resource scope with a lifetime, like the match, that frees everything it owns when it closes. Files load through one cache, and texture copies in main memory are released once they are on the graphics card (mesh copies too, behind a flag today). The design is in docs/memory-architecture.md, and CI measures whether a match leaves anything behind.

On low-memory devices, and in Safari, locations stream in near the player and the farthest ones are freed, with a cheap stand-in drawn in their place. That is what keeps a 16 GB Mac's Safari tab alive, and it's one of the formal models below.

What checks it

  • resource scopes Resource scopes not disposing their geometry, material and texture when closed, in order, or the ledger miscounting bytes by category.
  • lint Shared code that isn't deterministic, per-tick allocation in hot files, unowned GPU resources, raw URL flags, type-only imports written as values.
  • Low-memory plane queues the locations in view In low-memory mode, the plane queuing locations that are out of view or fewer than are in view (up to 2), or the chase camera seeing locations on too few paths.
  • no-GPU boot smoke A production build that doesn't boot in software-rendered Chromium (smoke only, not frame rate or looks), or holds more memory at the title than its budget.
  • no-GPU match-to-match memory Memory that grows from one match to the next, or resources no scope owns.
  • no-GPU low-memory memory More memory than budget in the low-memory setup: at the title, in the plane and 60 s into play.
  • no-GPU context restore A WebGL context lost at the title or in a match warm-up that doesn't restore.

Formal models (TLA+)

Some bugs only show up in an unlucky order of events, which tests rarely find. For the parts where that is most costly, I write a small TLA+ model of the code and let a model checker try every order. Each model below says what it proves, which rules it checks, and which code it covers. The diagrams are drawn from the model files or from the checked-in statecharts at build time. The "formal" step of npm test fails when the code a model describes changes after the model last passed, so a model can't keep passing about code that no longer exists.

6
models
in tools/formal
32
rules proved
always-true or eventually-true
34
deliberate breakages caught
each model must fail on every one

Client lifecycle

Client lifecycle: loading screen, title, practice and online matches, the waiting area, and WebGL context loss and restore.

Rules it proves

  • NoMatchWithoutRenderer always A match on screen always has its renderer.
  • LeaveFreesTheSeat always Once you are back on the title, the server no longer holds a seat in a match for you.
  • ButtonsAnswer always Pressing PLAY, CREATE or JOIN always does something the player can see.
  • ScopeHasOwner always The match's resource scope is open only while a match view (GameRender) owns it, so the next PLAY can open its own.
  • NoFrozenMatch always A match on screen is one the server still plays for this player (offline matches always are).

tools/formal/ClientLifecycle.tla covers 20 code regions and is tried against 6 deliberate breakages. The formal step of npm test fails if any region changes after the model last passed.

Match phases

Match phases with TLA+ (Warmup, Plane, Play, Results, over) - only the legal phase changes, a warm-up never longer than WARMUP_S however long a client streams, one winner on the results screen, and the liveness rule "a started online match ends".

A practice match loops back to the warm-up; an online match ends after the results.

Rules it proves

  • WarmupBounded always The warm-up never lasts longer than a full warm-up, however long a client streams (Match.warmWall)
  • OneWinner always The results screen has one winning squad, or none (all wiped at once)
  • OverFromResults always A match is over only from its results screen
  • PhaseOrder always
  • MatchEnds eventually A started online match ends: its loop stops and the players are back in the waiting area (practice loops by design)
  • PlayEnds eventually Every Play reaches its results (practice included)

tools/formal/MatchPhases.tla covers 23 code regions and is tried against 3 deliberate breakages. The formal step of npm test fails if any region changes after the model last passed.

Vehicle seats

Vehicle seats (tuk-tuks and helicopters): v.seats and each rider's st/veh/seat must always agree, one squad per vehicle, no dead rider.

This model has no checked-in statechart, so the table lists the steps the model allows, read from VehicleSeats.tla.

StepWhat it does in the game
EnteruseVehicle: freeSeat then enterVehicle (vehicle.ts)
GetOutstepRide (player.hot.ts): E pressed, or the vehicle is not on its wheels any more: exitVehicle; a vehicle already Gone is passed as null, so its seat is not touched
SwitchstepRide: crouch (switchSeat) or a seat key (takeSeat), vehicle.ts
Diekill: frees the seat if it is still this kong's, then veh = -1, st = Dead
Tipa tuk-tuk goes over (vehicle.ts stepVehicle/stepTumble set VS.Tipped and VE.TIP); the riders are thrown by tukEvents a moment later, or by their own stepRide first
Sinkthe water takes it (VS.Sunk and VE.SUNK); tukEvents ejects everyone
EventstukEvents: ejectAll on TIP or SUNK
BlowblowTuk: ejectAll, then a wreck
ClearstepVehicles: a wreck or a sunk vehicle is cleared away, or (warm-up) a fresh one spawns on its spot
FlipuseVehicle on a tipped tuk-tuk: flipVehicle; Righted when stepRighting finishes
HealstepVehicles: a seat whose kong is no longer Ride on this vehicle and seat is freed
PhaseenterWarmup / enterPlane: spawnTuks (vehs.reset, then fresh vehicles) and resetForMatch on every player
Respawna dead kong comes back on foot (warm-up respawn, redeploy, buy-back)

Rules it proves

  • SeatsAgree always A seat names a kong exactly when that kong rides this vehicle in this seat (the two copies agree)
  • NoDeadRider always No dead kong holds a seat
  • OneSquad always One squad per vehicle
  • RideOnWheels always A kong rides only a vehicle on its wheels, or one that has just gone over or under and is about to throw it out

tools/formal/VehicleSeats.tla covers 24 code regions and is tried against 4 deliberate breakages. The formal step of npm test fails if any region changes after the model last passed.

Low-memory residency

Low-memory POI streaming: which streamed locations hold memory, when one is evicted, and the cap.

Rules it proves

  • AtMostCapPlusOne always The same rule with one POI of slack: the one being built while the others still finish.
  • NoEvictWhileBuilding always A location is never thrown away while it is still building or fading in.
  • NothingPickedOutsideMatch always Nothing new is picked to build outside a match (title, waiting area, results screen).
  • GlideTargetFirst always While gliding, the POI the glide heads for builds before any queued POI behind it or to the side (RAY-272).
  • GlideTargetKept always Freeing space never throws away the POI the glide heads for while one behind it or to the side stays.

tools/formal/PoiResidency.tla covers 9 code regions and is tried against 5 deliberate breakages. The formal step of npm test fails if any region changes after the model last passed.

Crash heartbeat across tabs

Player diagnostics (KONG-71, RAY-162): the crash heartbeat across tabs (no false crash prompt, no lost crash, one report per crash) and the send flow (consent first, callsign only when ticked, every send answered, and the automatic summary, on by default for every player: none before the toast was shown, none after the player turned it off in Settings or under a privacy signal, none from automation) - against the code in client/src/playtest/beat.ts, diag.ts and report.ts.

Rules it proves

  • NoFalseCrash always The title never says "your last session closed unexpectedly" about a session that is still open, or that ended cleanly.
  • NoLostCrash always A session that dies after its first beat is picked up by a later load: until then the evidence is still in localStorage. A tab killed before main.ts runs (while the boot JS downloads and parses) leaves no record (see the skill).
  • OneReportPerCrash always One crash is reported at most once, however many tabs load and whatever the player taps.

tools/formal/DiagHeartbeat.tla covers 14 code regions and is tried against 4 deliberate breakages. The formal step of npm test fails if any region changes after the model last passed.

Sending a diagnostics report

Player diagnostics (KONG-71, RAY-162): the crash heartbeat across tabs (no false crash prompt, no lost crash, one report per crash) and the send flow (consent first, callsign only when ticked, every send answered, and the automatic summary, on by default for every player: none before the toast was shown, none after the player turned it off in Settings or under a privacy signal, none from automation) - against the code in client/src/playtest/beat.ts, diag.ts and report.ts.

Rules it proves

  • NoManualSendWithoutConsent always Nothing a player sends by hand leaves the browser before they have seen the consent text on the sheet.
  • CallsignOnlyWhenTicked always The callsign goes only in a send where "Include my callsign" was ticked.
  • AutoOnlyAfterNotice always An automatic summary leaves only after the toast was shown (or the player chose in Settings).
  • AutoRespectsOff always ... and never after the player turned it off in Settings or while the browser's privacy signal is on.
  • AutoNeverInAutomation always A page under automation sends nothing unless the URL or build asked for diagnostics.
  • NoBeatUnderSignal always The default stores no heartbeat under the browser's privacy signal; only an explicit ?diag does.
  • EverySendAnswered always Every send ends with something on screen: the thank-you with the report id, or a message that it did not go.
  • SendEnds eventually ... and a send never hangs: the player always sees one of the two in the end.
  • NoBeatAfterOff eventually ... and a record that outlives a switch-off in Settings is deleted by the next write (within one 5 s beat), unless the player switched back on first.

tools/formal/DiagSend.tla covers 26 code regions and is tried against 12 deliberate breakages. The formal step of npm test fails if any region changes after the model last passed.

What guards every PR

Every PR runs the whole npm test list and these CI jobs before it can land, plus an AI review. This table is generated from tools/run-tests.mjs and .github/workflows/ci.yml, so a new check shows up here the next time the dashboard is built. Where a check enforces numbers, the budget file is named; budgets only go down.

CheckWhat it catchesRunsBudget file
Every check is described on the How it's built pageA check in npm test or a CI job with no description in tools/dashboard/guards.json, or a description for one that no longer exists.fast·
typesA type error anywhere in the project (tsc --noEmit).fast·
lintShared code that isn't deterministic, per-tick allocation in hot files, unowned GPU resources, raw URL flags, type-only imports written as values.fasttools/lint/baseline.json
TLA+ models still match the code they describeA TLA+ model, or the code regions it names, changing since the model last passed its checker. It compares hashes of the code; it does not re-run the checker.fast·
feature flagsFeature-flag defaults, URL and stored overrides, and the query string the registry builds, not behaving as documented.fast·

swimmingSwimming in open deep water changing: floating at the surface, stroke speed, drawing and stowing the gun, and diving.fast·
kong faceIdle blinks (12 to 40 a minute, never in sync across 50 kongs), expressions reaching their targets within 0.3 s, or gaze going past its limits.fast·

path solverCapsule solver acceptance tests: the real step code against test boxes and against stuck spots found in live matches, each also run on the old solver for comparison.slow·
glassBreakable glass: every way to break a pane (shot, punch, sprint, rocket), window vaults, and the break events on the wire, including for a late joiner.slow·

raycast tiesStaticWorld.raycast disagreeing with a reference walk: exact ties between boxes and thousands of seeded random rays must give the same hit.fast·
resource scopesResource scopes not disposing their geometry, material and texture when closed, in order, or the ledger miscounting bytes by category.fast·
display refresh estimateThe display refresh estimate: a slow game must still read as the screen's real rate (60, 120, 144 Hz), and real 30 Hz pacing must read 30.fast·
half-rate guard decisionsThe half-rate guard lowering 3D resolution when it shouldn't, going below Auto's floor, not stepping back up after full-rate seconds, or oscillating.fast·
visibility gate lifecycleThe visibility gate: a gated object must hide while any gate is active and go back to a plain value once the last one is removed (a leftover gate once made a far stand-in vanish in one frame).fast·
HLOD captures a POI's far stateA POI's far proxy (engine/hlod.ts) never built because its module hides some of its own roots at range (a near model behind its far proxy, LOD rings), a proxy captured while terrain occlusion hides the POI, or a proxy that keeps drawing after its module hid what it merged.fast·
wire / matrix / geometry / http / splat parityFive checks, each asserted against its own expected result: network snapshots, the matrix cache, the geometry index, static file serving and splat viewport selection.slow·
host allocation per tick (against tools/alloc-budgets.json)Bytes allocated per host tick, or garbage collections, over the 7,200 play ticks of the seeded 50-bot match going over the ceiling, or more than the allowed margin under it until the ceiling is lowered.slowtools/alloc-budgets.json

What changed and why it matters

Survives the whole match

A 16 GB Mac can play a whole match in Safari

Before: Reached Safari's limit about 80 s after landing

How we know

Measured: Safari on a 16 GB Mac

Before, the game kept every location it had built, so memory only went up. The match reached Safari's limit on a 16 GB Mac (Safari closes a tab that passes it) about 80 seconds after the player landed. The game now keeps at most four locations at a time and drops the farthest ones as the player moves on. In the newest test below it reached the results screen both times, with peak memory about 1 GB lower than the version before it.

What you'll notice: on a 16 GB Mac in Safari, the match no longer ends with the tab closing on you.

Mac mini M4, 16 GB, Safari 27, quality Auto (picked Low), ?seed=42, scripted moving player, production build served locally. Newest: main 3248912, 2 runs. Before: main 1ee1f52, 1 run. Details in the Safari panel below.

Changes: #140, #149, #157, #160

1,543 MB

Textures are stored smaller, with no visible loss at the default

Before: 1,751 MB

How we know

Measured: texture memory, four heavy locations

The game now shrinks the textures (the pictures wrapped around 3D objects, like the stone on a temple wall) to 1024 pixels on their longest side, or to 512 pixels in Safari and on low-memory computers. In a test with four heavy locations loaded at the title, texture memory fell from 1,751 and 1,735 MB (cap off, two runs) to 1,543 and 1,515 MB at the default, and to 1,387 MB at 512.

What you'll notice: at 1024 pixels we saw no visible loss when comparing views at 3× zoom. At 512 pixels there is slight softening up close only (for example the nearest container logo at 3× zoom), not at normal size.

Memory: memory.mts without a GPU (SwiftShader, 640×360) at the title, 4 heavy locations, runs interleaved; WebGL textures 1751.4 and 1735.4 MB off, 1542.8 and 1514.8 MB default, 1387.1 MB at 512 (fork #158). Look: Kong RTX on Windows (D3D11), views compared at 3× crops (RAY-140, RAY-141).

Changes: #154, #156, #158

2.2 s

Coming back to the game after minimising is faster in Safari

Before: 9.9 s

How we know

Measured: time to ready after 120 s minimised

Safari stops drawing frames for a hidden window, and the game used to wait for those frames before it carried on loading. It now keeps going without them. After a window had been minimised for 120 seconds, the time until the game was ready again went from 9.9 s to 2.2 s.

What you'll notice: switching away and back lands you in the game in about 2 seconds instead of about 10.

A/B of fork #37 in Safari, recorded on RAY-112 (minimised for 120 s, time to ready). The machine and number of runs are on that issue, not on this page.

Changes: #37

Chrome and Windows numbers

How we know

The earlier work on Chrome and Windows (title screen load, first frame of a match, whole-browser memory, server work per tick) is in the Summary and Performance tabs, each with a before and after.

What you'll notice: a faster title screen and a smoother start to each match; the Summary tab lists each one in the same words.

Each number on those tabs carries its own method and source.

One scripted player (it drops near the harbor, then keeps moving toward the next safe place) was played until the match ended or reached Safari's limit. Landing came at 103 to 106 s in every run. Peak WebContent is the size of the part of Safari that runs the game's page, which is the part Safari closes. Times below are seconds since the test started.

In between: the version from #149 (e24cb9c) reached Results in 1 of 2 runs, and a version of #157 (14ecb8b) in 1 of 3. The other runs were killed for memory.

Two runs on one Mac are a signal, not a guarantee. The peaks, 7.3 and 6.9 GB, sit about 1 GB below the earlier build and at least about 0.7 GB below the lowest memory at which we saw a kill on this Mac (8.0 to 8.8 GB). That is better than before, but still not a wide margin. In run 1 the scripted player died once after getting stuck on a patch of terrain; that is a limit of the script, and the run still reached Results.

The journey so far
  1. Nov 3 #37 Safari keeps loading when its window is hidden, instead of waiting for frames it will not draw.
  2. Nov 5 #140 Low-memory mode builds the locations in view from the starting islet and the plane, and measures range along the ground.
  3. Nov 5 #149 Low-memory mode drops the farthest locations once a match is in play, so memory stops climbing.
  4. Nov 5 #154 A texture size cap is added behind a flag (off by default).
  5. Nov 5 #156 The harbor locations' painted textures follow the same cap.
  6. Nov 5 #157 Locations are ranked by where the player will be in 5 seconds, and builds are spaced out while moving fast.
  7. Nov 5 #158 The texture cap turns on by default: 1024 pixels, or 512 in Safari and on low-memory computers.
  8. Nov 5 #160 Building a location and dropping one now use the same ranking. In the Safari test, both runs reached Results and peak memory fell by about 1 GB.
Words used on this page
Memory
The working space a program uses while it runs. A browser tab that uses too much of it gets slow, or gets closed.
Killed for memory
Safari (and other browsers) close a tab that grows past a limit instead of letting the whole computer slow down. For a player, the game simply disappears mid-match.
WebContent
The part of Safari that runs the game's page. Its size is the number to watch, because it is the part Safari closes.
Location (streaming a location)
A named place on the island, such as a harbor or a temple. The game builds each one as the player gets close, which is called streaming it in. A location the game has built and still holds is called resident.
Texture
A picture wrapped around a 3D object, like the stone pattern on a temple wall. Big textures look sharper and use more memory, mostly on the graphics card (GPU memory).
Frame time
How long the computer takes to draw one picture of the game. Smaller is smoother, and a long one shows up as a stutter. The Performance tab is full of these.

Since v0.2.0, the project has made the game faster to load, smoother to start and cheaper to run, with every change measured before and after.

Memory over time

How much memory the game makes the browser use, second by second, from launch to the results screen. Each line is one run.

Safari on a 16 GB Mac mini: main vs v0.5.0

Safari stops the game's page when its WebContent process gets too big: at 8,473 MB and 8,793 MB in these runs. Both runs where the kong moved around were stopped: main 55 seconds after landing, and v0.5.0 before it had even landed. The run where the kong stood still lasted to the results screen at 8,049 MB. Each step up is a new location loading, and nothing is released afterwards.

Chrome on Windows (D3D11): v0.2.0 vs main

Three runs of each build with the fixed measuring script, both standing still. At every measured phase, main 8f42339's median is 1,604 to 2,135 MB lower than kong-v0.2.0's: 6,504 MB against 8,409 MB at the title, 12,304 MB against 14,426 MB thirty seconds into a match, and 12,500 MB against 14,506 MB after leaving the second match. Neither build grows from one match to the next. The two builds don't run at the same quality: on Auto, v0.2.0 boots at ultra and main boots at high. Comparing with the earlier ultra and high runs on this machine suggests about 1,700 MB of the gap comes from our releases and about 350 MB from the lower quality, but that split is an estimate across two days of runs, not a same-quality test.

Where the numbers come from
  • kong-v0.2.0 (Auto boots ultra): project drive: handoffs/memory-v020-vs-main-d3d11/v020-1/result.json and README.md (RAY-138); result.json source.commit names the tool checkout, not the served build
  • main 8f42339 (Auto boots high): project drive: handoffs/memory-v020-vs-main-d3d11/main-1/result.json and README.md (RAY-138); result.json source.commit names the tool checkout, not the served build
  • project drive: handoffs/memory-v020-vs-main-d3d11/README.md (medians, quality tiers, release vs quality split) and v020-1, main-1 result.json (RAY-138); the chart shows run 1 of each

Chrome vs Safari on the same 16 GB Mac mini

Both runs leave the kong standing still. Chrome levels off at about 10 GB for the whole browser (9,943 MB median 60 seconds into a match, six runs) and doesn't grow in a second match. Safari keeps climbing as locations load and reaches 9,278 MB by the results screen. Chrome's total counts every browser process. Safari's counts only the page's process and its graphics process, so Safari's real total is higher than shown. The two runs are on different builds: main 7890f3b for Chrome, main f417032 for Safari. The Chrome run ends at 320 seconds. It plays two matches and leaves each one about 60 seconds after landing (the first runs from Play at 34 seconds to leaving at 178 seconds). It doesn't play a match through to the results screen, so it doesn't show Chrome over a full match.

Swap and memory pressure (Chrome runs 4 to 6): about 2.5 GB of swap was already in use before each run, and it never rose during one (peaks of 2,571, 2,539 and 2,499 MB, each the starting value). macOS reported memory pressure as "warn" at every sample and never "critical".

Where the numbers come from
  • Chrome 154, main 7890f3b: project drive: handoffs/memory-baseline-metal-v3/run4/result.json; swap and pressure from sys-run4.jsonl (README.md)
  • Safari 27, main f417032: project drive: handoffs/safari-growth/kmt/f417032-r1-idle.json; KONG-54 tracer.mjs f417-r1/trace.json; totalMB = WebContent + WebKit GPU process phys_footprint (Safari UI and networking processes not counted)
  • project drive: handoffs/memory-baseline-metal-v3/README.md (medians, swap, pressure) and handoffs/safari-growth/README.md

Low-memory mode on vs off (Chrome on Windows, D3D11)

Low-memory mode (?lowmem=1) waits to build each location until the player gets near it, but it never unloads one. It only saves memory early on: in the plane it held about 7,100 MB against about 13,300 MB with it off. Memory climbs from the moment the kong lands. After about 2 km travelled (the plane, the drop and one leg of walking) it already holds 21 of the 26 locations, and by 4 km the two lines have met (about 14,200 MB against 13,700 MB). Both runs end at about 13,300 MB on the results screen, and the peak is only about 200 MB lower with it on. These runs used the older measuring script. On this Windows machine the fixed script gave the same totals as the older one, so the numbers hold.

Where the numbers come from
  • lowmem on, main b542346: project drive: handoffs/lowmem-growth-d3d11/cdp/cdp-lowmem1/growth.json and README.md (RAY-122); totalMB is every Chrome process (WorkingSet64)
  • lowmem off, main b542346: project drive: handoffs/lowmem-growth-d3d11/cdp/cdp-lowmem0/growth.json and README.md (RAY-122); totalMB is every Chrome process (WorkingSet64)
  • project drive: handoffs/lowmem-growth-d3d11/README.md (distance table, module counts) and cdp/samples.csv, cdp/*/growth.json (plane-phase samples) (RAY-122); the overstatement is KONG-43; v3 confirmation for D3D11: project drive handoffs/memory-baseline-d3d11-v3/README.md (RAY-130)

Chrome on Windows (D3D11) with the fixed measuring script: main vs v0.4.1

Three runs of each build with the fixed measuring script, both standing still. At every measured phase, main 7890f3b's median was lower: 6,091 MB against 8,063 MB at the title, 12,364 MB against 12,718 MB thirty seconds into a match, and 12,631 MB against 12,812 MB after leaving the second match. The chart shows one run of each, and between those phases the two lines sometimes cross. The two builds don't run at the same quality, though. Since #125, main boots at high on Auto on this machine, while v0.4.1 boots at ultra, and that change accounts for most of the gap at the title.

Chrome on Windows (D3D11): v0.4.0 vs v0.4.1

The release measurements found v0.4.1 used 469 MB less than v0.4.0 thirty seconds into a match (13,188 to 12,719 MB, median of three runs each). These runs used the older measuring script, which overstated totals on the Mac. Rerunning v0.4.1 with the fixed script gave 12,718 MB at the same point, against 12,764 MB from the older script, so these Windows numbers hold.
